concept_name: A point and a line segment from a crease

item.question: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.)
steps: Fold the paper and open it.
The crease is straight and has two ends: A and B.
item.answer: Yes, the crease is a straight mark; it gives the idea of a line segment with two end points A and B.
item.text:
Worked example: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.)
1. Fold the paper and open it.
2. The crease is straight and has two ends: A and B.
Answer: Yes, the crease is a straight mark; it gives the idea of a line segment with two end points A and B.

concept_name: The shortest route from A to B

item.question: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1). What is the shortest route from A to B?
steps: Draw several routes from A to B (zig-zag, curved).
Compare lengths; the straight route is shortest.
This shortest path including A and B is the line segment AB.
item.answer: The straight path from A to B, which is the line segment AB.
item.text:
Worked example: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1). What is the shortest route from A to B?
1. Draw several routes from A to B (zig-zag, curved).
2. Compare lengths; the straight route is shortest.
3. This shortest path including A and B is the line segment AB.
Answer: The straight path from A to B, which is the line segment AB.

item.question: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (Fig. 2.2). Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?

concept_name: A ray starts at a point

item.question: A torch at T shines a beam towards a lamp post L. The beam goes past L and never stops. Is the beam a line segment, a ray or a line? Name it.
steps: The beam starts at T, a fixed starting point.
It passes through L and goes on in one direction without end.
A part of a line with one starting point is a ray.
The starting point comes first in the name, so the beam is ray TL.
item.answer: It is a ray, named TL, with starting point T.
item.text:
Worked example: A torch at T shines a beam towards a lamp post L. The beam goes past L and never stops. Is the beam a line segment, a ray or a line? Name it.
1. The beam starts at T, a fixed starting point.
2. It passes through L and goes on in one direction without end.
3. A part of a line with one starting point is a ray.
4. The starting point comes first in the name, so the beam is ray TL.
Answer: It is a ray, named TL, with starting point T.

concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

item.question: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
steps: The two legs are the arms.
The joint where they meet is the vertex.
item.answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.
item.text:
Worked example: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
1. The two legs are the arms.
2. The joint where they meet is the vertex.
Answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.

concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

item.question: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
steps: The blades are the arms.
The pivot screw is the vertex.
item.answer: The two blades are the arms; the vertex is the screw/pivot where the blades are joined.
item.text:

concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

item.question: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
steps: Find the two parts that turn about a hinge.
Those parts are the arms; the hinge is the vertex.
item.answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).
